author: Eric Rosane
title: 'Some freedom again.' Murdered Pasco bus driver's family finally finds 'relief' - NewsBreak
text:
By Eric Rosane ,
4 hours ago Joshua D. Davis talks with his attorney during his sentencing hearing in Franklin County on July 29. He murdered Richard “Dick” Lenhart on a school bus, in front of more than 30 students in 2021. Scott Hunt, Special to the Herald The 39-year-old Richland man convicted of stabbing to death a Pasco School District bus driver in 2021 was sentenced Wednesday to nearly 42 years in prison.
Joshua D. Davis sat motionless, staring down, as Judge Jackie Shea-Brown read her judgment in a Franklin County Superior Court courtroom in Pasco.
He was flanked by three sheriff's deputies, and spoke only to acknowledge his rights to appeal and that he may not possess a firearm when released.
Joshua D. Davis talks with his attorney during his sentencing hearing in Franklin County on July 29. He murdered Richard “Dick” Lenhart on a school bus, in front of more than 30 students in 2021. Scott Hunt, Special to the Herald Across the room, widow Nancy Lenhart and other family members broke down in tears with emotion as the sentence was read. The moment marked 1,772 days — or four years, 10 months and five days — since Richard “Dick” Lenhart was murdered on a school bus, in front of 35 children, outside Longfellow Elementary in September 2021.
“For elementary students, a school bus driver is far more than just a person who drives them to and from school,” Shea-Brown said.
Superior Court Judge Jackie Shea-Brown sentences Joshua Davis for the 2021 murder of Richland “Dick” Lenhart, a Pasco school bus driver. Scott Hunt, Special to the Herald “They are a trusted guardian, mentor and friend who shapes the start and end of each day... Someone who makes the bus ride a part of the day to look forward to, and helps them feel seen, valued and ready to learn, and no doubt that was what Mr. Lenhart was to those children.”
A poster board with images of Richard Lenhart in his bus and with family was stagged across the room from Davis.
Shea-Brown said despite a schizophrenia diagnosis and a traumatic childhood, Davis was a cognizant party to the crime and could tell right from wrong. While he tried to get help for his mental health illness, he did not do so in an adequate fashion.
Widow Nancy Lenhart, right, gets a hug during the emotional sentencing of her husband’s murderer. Joshua D. Davis killed Richard “Dick” Lenhart on a school bus in front of more than 30 students in 2021. Scott Hunt, Special to the Herald After the sentence hearing, Nancy Lenhart told news media that Wednesday marked the end of a chapter for their family. Their lives have been “on hold,” month by month, and today gave them some resolution to move forward.
“I think this is the closing of a chapter. The book will never be fully closed, it will always be there,” Nancy Lenhart said.
“Grief is nothing that ever goes away, but you learn how to live with it, and you learn how to travel with it. I invited mine in, we sat down and had a cup of tea together, and decided how we’re going to live together,” she said.
She thanked the Tri-City community for the support, as well as first responders, the Pasco School District, Franklin County Prosecutor’s Office and other bus drivers. She hopes the sentence helps the affected families and children find some “peace and closure.”
Prosecutor Shawn Sant sits near a poster board with images of Richard Lenhart in his bus and with family during the murder sentencing for Joshua Davis in Pasco. Scott Hunt, Special to the Herald “We may not be happy for as long as it took to get here, but this shows that the process is still working and, in the end, justice is obtained,” she said. “It’s a release now. We feel like we have some freedom again, and we haven’t had that for almost five years. It’s a relief.”
A jury convicted Davis in November of premeditated first-degree murder with a deadly weapon and aggravated factors following a three-week trial.
While Davis pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity , jurors found he understood what he was doing and that it was wrong.
He faced a standard sentencing range of 22 to 28 years in prison. Prosecutors argued the nature of Davis’ crime warranted an exceptional of 50 years, while the defense asked for 25.
The court recommended at sentencing that he be treated at a special offender unit at the Monroe Correctional Complex, though it will be up to the state Department of Correction where he is sent next.
Davis also was ordered to pay about $9,400 in restitution to Lenhart’s widow. Another $138,000 in restitution to the Southeast Washington Workers Compensation Trust was questioned by the defense and may require an additional hearing, likely in October.
Pasco school bus Scott Hunt, Special to the Herald A beloved bus driver and father Nancy Lenhart’s journey to seek justice for her slain husband has taken her and her family to more places than courtrooms.
Trespassing on a public school bus is now a gross misdemeanor in Washington state thanks to the passage of the 2024 Richard Lenhart Act.
Nancy Lenhart suddenly found herself an advocate for bus safety, and she championed the legislation to the governor’s desk. She’s still hoping to “take it federal” so that the protections can apply to all 50 states.
The Pasco School Board also approved naming the new Stearman Avenue bus barn that opened in 2023 the “Richard L. Lenhart Transportation Center.”
The Pasco School Board renamed the new Stearman Avenue bus barn that opened in 2023 the “Richard L. Lenhart Transportation Center.” Scott Hunt, Special to the Herald Still, Nancy Lenhart and her family have been at every hearing and court appearance since Richard’s passing.
“We never dreamed that our journey through the justice system would be a trial of patience, strength and endurance. But we’ve finally reached the day of justice’s deliverance for us, justice for Richard and consequences received by his murderer,” she said.
Lenhart, who died at age 72, is remembered as a selfless, generous and gentle father, husband and co-worker. Nancy and Richard Lenhart had been married for 40 years.
He worked six years with the school district and drove Route 4, convinced he had found a second calling late in life.
A school bus full of kids crashed in 2021 afternoon at Longfellow Elementary School after the driver, Richard Lenhart, was stabbed by a man. Cameron Probert/Tri-City Herald Stabbing outside Longfellow Elementary Richard Lenhart was killed on Sept. 24, 2021, while picking up students at the end of the school day.
Davis had driven his truck to a neighborhood near the school and parked it about 3 p.m. As Lenhart was about to leave with his kids, Davis ran toward the bus and prompted Lenhart to open the bus doors in anticipation of a question.
Davis boarded the bus and asked if it was going to Road 100. When Lenhart said it wasn’t, Davis turned around to pull out a knife and stabbed him 13 times. He left the bus and waited nearby for police to arrive.
Lenhart died later at the hospital.
Shea-Brown said the letter Davis left his mother the day of the attack and his boarding of the bus before asking his question were “all actions, very goal oriented and intentional.” She said he was not intoxicated during the attack, and that he is generally a “good historian” of events.
Richard Lenhart, 72, was a school bus driver for the Pasco School District for six years. Courtesy the Lenhart family The murder sent shockwaves through the Pasco community, and sparked an outpouring of support for Lenhart and Pasco’s nearly 100 bus drivers.
Nancy Lenhart says she has shared messages of sympathy and condolences with Davis’ mother.
“They’re victims, too,” she said. “We’ve let them know that we don’t hold the family to blame for anything because he’s responsible for his own actions.”
Davis’ 500 months served for his murder includes a base sentence of 300 months, or 25 years, plus an additional 24 months for the deadly weapon enhancement.
Shea-Brown imposed an additional 156 months, or 13 years, for the aggravators that Davis’ conduct resulted in deliberate cruelty to the victim, and the offense involved a foreseeable and destructible impact on persons other than the victim.
